discovery: Discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos and the opening of neutrino astronomy with the IceCube Neutrino Observatory
motivation: Francis Halzen conceived and led IceCube, a cubic-kilometre detector in the Antarctic ice that opened a new observational window on the energetic universe. In 2013 IceCube discovered a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies. It went on to identify individual sources: the flaring blazar TXS 0506+056 (2017-18), the active galaxy NGC 1068 (2022), and neutrino emission from the Milky Way's Galactic plane (2023). Because neutrinos travel undeflected and unabsorbed, these results give direct, quantitative evidence of where hadronic cosmic rays are accelerated. That is a problem that photon and charged-particle observations could not settle alone. The work turned a decades-old idea into a working astronomy and connected cosmic-ray, gamma-ray and X-ray studies of compact objects, galactic nuclei and star-forming galaxies. It also established multimessenger astrophysics as a quantitative discipline.
